extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis / Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and structural estimates used to classify and control singularities of the Ricci flow on compact orientable three-manifolds (canonical neighborhoods, pinching, noncollapsing, rescaling limits, and curvature/volume estimates). Includes the singularity structure theorem and elliptic-type curvature estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalized metric
rubrics_metrics.description: A Riemannian metric on a compact orientable three-manifold is called normalized if the eigenvalues of its curvature operator at every point are bounded by 1/10, and every geodesic ball of radius one has volume at least one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization of the initial metric is used to guarantee the pinching estimate and to obtain κ-noncollapsing properties for subsequent rescalings; after rescaling one may assume the initial metric is normalized so the arguments below apply (e.g. existence on a maximal time interval [0,t_max) with t_max > 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood classification for ancient κ-solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: For an arbitrarily given ε > 0, each point in an ancient κ-solution has a neighborhood which is either an evolving ε-neck, or an evolving ε-cap, or a compact (without boundary) positively curved manifold (a metric quotient of the round S^3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6 referenced) further supplies quantitative control: in the neck/cap cases one may find radii r with B_t(x,r) ⊂ B_t(x,2r) and scalar curvature on the neighborhood between C_2^{-1}R(x,t) and C_2 R(x,t) (constants C1(ε), C2(ε) from Theorem 6.4.6). In the cap/neck cases a scaled volume estimate is required: (C_2 R(x,t))^{-3/2} Vol_t(B) ≤ ε r^3 (used to rule out certain counterexamples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity structure theorem (Theorem 7.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0 and T0>1 there exists r0>0 so that for any solution to Ricci flow on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric (defined up to time ≥ T0), and for any point (x0,t0) with t0 ≥ 1 and Q = R(x0,t0), the solution in the appropriate parabolic neighborhood around (x0,t0) (of size comparable to Q^{-1/2} in space and Q^{-1} in time) is, after scaling by factor Q, ε-close (in the C^{[ε^{-1}]} topology) to the corresponding subset of some orientable ancient κ-solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the precise local-model criterion: high-curvature regions (when viewed at the curvature scale) must be close to ancient κ-solutions. The statement gives the scale and topology for closeness (C^{[ε^{-1}]}). The theorem underpins canonical neighborhood assertions for singularities coming from sequences of high-curvature points.

rubrics_metrics.name: κ-noncollapsing / Perelman's no local collapsing
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions with normalized initial metric (and in the context of Theorem 7.1.1) are κ-noncollapsed on all scales less than √T0 (and, for limits, κ-noncollapsed on all scales for some positive κ depending on T0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: κ-noncollapsing supplies lower bounds on injectivity radius/volume at curvature scales and is essential to apply Hamilton compactness and obtain C^∞_loc limits after rescaling. It is invoked repeatedly to obtain uniform injectivity radius and volume control in rescaled neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pinching estimate (7.1.1) for three-dimensional normalized solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a solution with normalized initial metric the curvature operator satisfies a quantitative pinching estimate (displayed as (7.1.1)) relating Rm (eigenvalues λ, μ, ν) to the scalar curvature R and time: the negative part of the curvature operator is controlled by a function of R(1+t) (expressed via the convex increasing function f and its inverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pinching estimate guarantees that limits of appropriate rescalings have nonnegative curvature operator; it is used to exclude certain limit geometries and to deduce nonnegativity of sectional curvature in limits (cf. rewrite (7.1.2)). The pinching is used throughout to pass to limits that are ancient κ-solutions with nonnegative curvature operator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local derivative estimates in regions ε-close to ancient κ-solutions (Lemma 7.1.2 input)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a region of the solution is ε-close to an ancient κ-solution then derivative bounds hold on that segment: the gradient and time derivative of scalar curvature are small in the appropriate scaled sense (Theorem 6.4.3(ii) yields bounds of the form (normalized derivatives) ≤ 2η on those segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose ε sufficiently small (and correspondingly small c depending on η) so that integrating these derivative bounds along space-time segments yields local curvature control (Lemma 7.1.2): scalar curvature at nearby times/points stays within controlled multiples (e.g. R(x,t) ≤ 2 R(¯x,¯t) on suitable parabolic neighborhoods). This is a technical criterion to promote ε-closeness to quantitative curvature bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescaling and convergence criterion to obtain ancient κ-limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence of compact normalized solutions with points (x_k,t_k) where curvature blows up and Q_k = R(x_k,t_k), after rescaling by factors Q_k and shifting times, a subsequence converges in the C^∞_loc topology to a nonflat complete orientable ancient κ-solution provided one has the pinching estimate, κ-noncollapsing and local curvature controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard compactness/rescaling criterion: combine pinching, no-local-collapsing, local curvature derivative estimates and Hamilton compactness to extract limits. The limit classification (neck/cap/compact) then yields contradictions when the original sequence violates the canonical neighborhood conclusions, which is the backbone of many existence/structure proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic-type curvature estimate via local volume (Theorem 7.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any A<∞ there exist K=K(A) and α(A)>0 such that if a solution on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric satisfies on a parabolic region (0 ≤ t ≤ r0^2, d_0(x,x0) ≤ r0) the bound |Rm|(x,t) ≤ 2 r0^{-2} and r0 < α and the volume lower bound Vol_0(B_0(x0,r0)) ≥ A^{-1} r0^3, then R(x,r0^2) ≤ K r0^{-2} whenever d_{r0^2}(x,x0) < A r0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an elliptic-type estimate: a combination of a local curvature upper bound on a small parabolic region and a volume lower bound forces a uniform scalar curvature bound at later times over a larger spatial radius (or else the alternative is that a scaled neighborhood is ε-close to an orientable ancient κ-solution). The proof relies on Perelman's no local collapsing II, the singularity structure theorem, and the rescaling/convergence machinery above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance principle for curvature estimates (via volume growth and elliptic estimates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curvature estimates for ancient κ-solutions (elliptic-type estimates and curvature control via volume growth, e.g. Theorem 6.3.3 and Theorem 6.4.3) are heritable to general solutions on three-manifolds: near high-curvature points the solution looks like an ancient κ-solution and thus inherits its curvature/volume controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the singularity structure theorem to assert ε-closeness to ancient κ-solutions on curvature scales, then import quantitative estimates (curvature bounds, derivative bounds, volume estimates) from the ancient κ-solution setting to the general solution; this yields the key curvature controls used for surgery and long-time analysis.
